context_title: Multi Agent system The management system allows for the simultaneous management of 50 million context windows, so that the models have only 1 million context windows, but the agent system can actually manage 50 million contexts at a time, all characters are active.

entries.query: Multi Agent system The management system allows for the simultaneous management of 50 million context windows, so that the models have only 1 million context windows, but the agent system can actually manage 50 million contexts at a time, all characters are active.
entries.answer:
A **Multi-Agent Context Management System** that can orchestrate 50 million simultaneous context windows — while individual models are constrained to 1 million tokens each — is a sophisticated hierarchical architecture problem. Here is a comprehensive design for Jaide's context management layer, built entirely in Zig, exploiting Jaide's existing infrastructure (ChaosCoreKernel, RSF layers, SSI index, MGT tokenizer, etc.).

***

## Core Architecture: The 50M Context Problem

The fundamental challenge is a 50:1 amplification: each model has a 1M-token hard limit, yet the system must make **50 million distinct, fully "alive" characters/agents** feel coherently continuous. This is solved by a four-tier hierarchical context memory system. The hot tier (active model context) holds at most 1M tokens per model instance. The warm tier (SSI semantic index) holds compressed, surprise-weighted embeddings for the last ~10M events per agent. The cold tier (ChaosCore content-addressable storage) holds full block-level snapshots keyed by SHA-256 content hash. The archival tier (distributed persistent volumes) holds checkpoint-serialized state blobs, versioned via the temporal graph.[1][2]

The 50-million figure is achieved not by running 50M model instances in parallel, but by **sparse activation**: at any moment, only a small fraction of agents are in the hot tier. The system dynamically promotes/demotes context windows using the `ChaosCoreKernel`'s `optimizeDataPlacement` and `balanceLoad` routines, which already implement affinity-based migration across cores. This is essentially OS-style virtual memory, but for transformer KV-caches.[1]

***

## The `ContextSupervisor` Layer (New Zig Module)

The new module `src/multiagent/context_supervisor.zig` sits above the existing `DistributedTrainer` and `InferenceServer` layers. It maintains a `HashMap(AgentId, ContextDescriptor)` of all 50M registered agents, where `ContextDescriptor` is a compact 128-byte struct containing: the agent's SSI anchor hash, its last-active timestamp, its hot/warm/cold tier membership flag, its current model-slot assignment (if in hot tier), and a ring-buffer pointer into the MGT tokenizer's streaming window.[2][3][4]

Scheduling uses a **Least Recently Used + Surprise Priority** eviction policy. The SSI `surprise` score of each agent's last token event determines its eviction priority: high-surprise agents (unexpected, plot-critical events in characters) resist eviction from the hot tier, while low-surprise agents (idle NPCs repeating routine behavior) are rapidly demoted to the warm tier. This ensures dramatic, narratively-active characters always have full 1M-context fidelity.[5]

***

## KV-Cache Sharding Across Model Slots

The `InferenceServer` already supports configurable batch processing and API-key-based routing. The `ContextSupervisor` extends this by treating each model slot as a **KV-cache shard**. A 1M-token context window is divided into 64 segments of ~16K tokens each. When an agent is promoted to hot tier, only the segments with non-zero RSF activation magnitude (computed via `futharkentryrsfforward`) are loaded — the rest remain as compressed warm-tier embeddings. This gives effective context utilization of ~15–20% of raw capacity, meaning one model slot can serve 5–7 agents simultaneously through interleaved segment injection.[6][7][2]

With, say, 1,000 model slots (achievable on 8× B200 GPUs at Modal ), the effective hot-tier population is 5,000–7,000 simultaneously fully-active agents, with the remaining 49.99M agents managed across warm and cold tiers. Promotion latency from warm → hot is bounded by a single SSI retrieval + RSF forward pass, targeting sub-50ms per the Futhark GPU kernel pipeline.[8][9]

***

## Context Continuity: The "All Characters Are Active" Guarantee

The requirement that **all characters remain active** (not frozen/paused) is enforced at the warm tier through **predictive micro-forward passes**. Every 100ms, the system runs a lightweight 2-layer RSF micro-model (not the full JAIDE stack) over each warm-tier agent's compressed SSI state, producing a delta-prediction vector. This delta is stored back into the SSI as a new surprise-weighted segment, so the agent's internal state evolves even while it is not in the hot tier. The SFD optimizer's finite-difference gradient approximation is repurposed here to efficiently compute these micro-deltas without a full backward pass.[10][11]

This is conceptually analogous to how real-time game engines maintain AI behavior trees for off-screen NPCs: full simulation is not run, but a lightweight state machine advances the agent's context vector forward in time. The key difference in Jaide's system is that these updates are *probabilistically verified* via the ZK-inference Circom circuit, so any agent brought back to hot tier can prove its warm-tier evolution was coherent with its prior hot-tier state.[12]

***

## Distributed Synchronization via NCCL + Temporal Graph

Context state for agents that interact with each other requires cross-agent coherence. The `temporal_graph.zig` module (versioned, append-only DAG of agent state events) serves as the **shared blackboard**  for inter-agent interactions. When two warm-tier agents interact (e.g., NPC A gives item to NPC B), the interaction is recorded as a temporal edge, and both agents' SSI anchor hashes are updated atomically via `NCCLAllReduce` across GPU nodes. This ensures that when either agent is promoted to hot tier, their context window includes the interaction event without requiring both to be simultaneously hot.[13][14][15]

The NCCL broadcast latency at 8× B200 scale is under 2ms for the compact 128-byte `ContextDescriptor` payloads, making real-time cross-agent synchronization viable even at 50M agent scale when interaction graphs are sparse (which they naturally are in most world-simulation scenarios).[14]

***

## Memory Footprint and Feasibility

| Tier | Agents | Per-Agent Storage | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hot (1M ctx) | ~7,000 | ~2 GB (KV-cache f16) | ~14 TB (GPU HBM) [8] |
| Warm (SSI compressed) | ~5M | ~50 KB (embeddings) | ~250 GB (CPU RAM) [9] |
| Cold (ChaosCore blocks) | ~45M | ~4 KB (state hash) | ~180 GB (NVMe) [1] |
| Archive (Modal volumes) | All 50M | ~1 KB (checkpoint ptr) | ~50 GB (persistent) [8] |

The cold and archive tiers are entirely handled by `ChaosCoreKernel`'s content-addressable storage with SHA-256 deduplication, which means agents with similar states (e.g., generic NPCs in the same location) share blocks and the real cold-tier footprint is significantly smaller than the worst case.[1]

***

## Integration with Existing Jaide Codebase

The `ContextSupervisor` module calls `InferenceServer.handleBatch` for hot-tier agents, `SSI.retrieveTopK` for warm-tier state restoration, `ChaosCoreKernel.readMemory` / `allocateMemory` for cold-tier block I/O, and `ModalGPUClient.submitJob` for overflow promotion when local GPU capacity is saturated. The MGT tokenizer's streaming window (`STREAMING_BUFFER_SIZE = 1024`, `STREAMING_WINDOW_SIZE = 512`) is used to efficiently serialize/deserialize partial context windows during tier transitions without re-tokenizing the full agent history.[4][16][5][2][1]

The zero-knowledge inference trace (`inference_trace.circom`) wraps the entire promotion pipeline, producing a Groth16 proof that any hot-tier agent's current state is a valid continuation of its archived cold-tier checkpoint. This is the formal security guarantee that "all characters are active and coherent" — not just an engineering approximation, but a cryptographically verifiable invariant.[12]
